text: PepsiCo, Inc. is a leading global beverage and convenient food company that was incorporated in Delaware in 1919 and reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986. The company operates through seven reportable segments: Frito-Lay North America (FLNA), Quaker Foods North America (QFNA), PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA), Latin America (LatAm), Europe, Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA), and Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region (APAC). FLNA produces and sells branded convenient foods such as Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, and Tostitos, sold to independent distributors and retailers, and operates a joint venture with Strauss Group to market Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads. QFNA produces and sells cereals, rice, pasta, and other branded foods like Cap’n Crunch, Life cereal, Quaker grits, and Quaker oatmeal, distributed through independent distributors and retailers. PBNA manufactures and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods under brands such as Aquafina, Diet Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Pepsi, and Propel, operating its own bottling and distribution facilities and also supplying to authorized and independent bottlers. PBNA also produces ready-to-drink tea and coffee through joint ventures with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks, and manufactures brands licensed from Keurig Dr Pepper and Dole Food Company, Inc. and Ocean Spray Cranberries, Inc. In the first quarter of 2022, PepsiCo sold its Tropicana, Naked, and other select juice brands to PAI Partners while retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in a new joint venture that operates across North America and Europe, with PepsiCo acting as the exclusive distributor for small-format and foodservice customers in the U.S. with chilled direct-store-delivery. LatAm markets and sells convenient food brands including Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Quaker products, and beverage brands such as 7UP, Gatorade, Pepsi, and San Carlos, sold to authorized and independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers, and also produces ready-to-drink tea via a joint venture with Unilever. Europe markets and sells convenient food brands like Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Quaker products, beverage brands including 7UP, Diet Pepsi, Pepsi Max, and Pepsi, and also produces SodaStream sparkling water makers and dairy products such as Agusha, Chudo, and Domik v Derevne, with ready-to-drink tea via a joint venture with Unilever. AMESA markets and sells convenient food brands such as Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, and Quaker products, and beverage brands including 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, and Pepsi, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, with ready-to-drink tea via a joint venture with Unilever. APAC markets and sells convenient food brands including BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Smith’s, and beverage brands such as 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, and Sting, sold to authorized and independent bottlers and retailers, and also produces ready-to-drink tea through a joint venture with Unilever. The company serves customers and consumers in more than 200 countries and territories. The aggregate market value of PepsiCo, Inc. Common Stock held by nonaffiliates as of June 11, 2021, was $203.9 billion, based on the closing sale price on that date. The number of shares of PepsiCo, Inc. Common Stock outstanding as of February 3, 2022, was 1,383,451,400.

Products are sold to authorized and independent bottlers, independent distributors, and retailers. In certain markets, AMESA operates its own bottling plants and distribution facilities. AMESA, either independently or in collaboration with third parties, produces, markets, distributes, and sells ready-to-drink tea products through an international joint venture with Unilever under the Lipton brand name. In the Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China Region, APAC produces, markets, distributes, and sells a range of convenient food brands including BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, and Smith’s, as well as Quaker-branded convenient foods, through consolidated businesses and noncontrolled affiliates. APAC also produces, markets, distributes, and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods under brands such as 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, and Sting, which are sold to authorized and independent bottlers, independent distributors, and retailers. APAC also produces, markets, distributes, and sells ready-to-drink tea products through the same international joint venture with Unilever under the Lipton brand name. Additionally, APAC licenses the Tropicana brand for co-branded juice products in China through a strategic alliance with Tingyi (Cayman Islands) Holding Corp. (Tingyi). Products are primarily distributed through direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse systems, distributor networks, and e-commerce platforms and mobile applications, with the method depending on customer needs, product characteristics, and local trade practices. DSD involves delivering beverages and convenient foods directly to retail stores, where they are merchandised by company employees or independent bottlers, enabling high visibility and appeal, especially for frequently restocked items responsive to in-store promotion. Some products are delivered to customer warehouses from company or third-party manufacturing and distribution centers, which is less costly and suitable for less fragile, non-perishable items with lower turnover. Many products are distributed via third-party distributors, which are effective for achieving broad reach by including multiple product lines on delivery vehicles, such as in the foodservice and vending business that delivers to restaurants, businesses, schools, and stadiums. Products are also available directly to consumers on company-owned and third-party e-commerce websites and mobile commerce apps. Key ingredients include apple, orange, and pineapple juice and concentrates, aspartame, corn, corn sweeteners, flavorings, flour, grapefruit, other fruits, oats, potatoes, raw milk, rice, seasonings, sucralose, sugar, vegetable and essential oils, and wheat, with water used in manufacturing. Packaging materials include plastic resins such as polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and polypropylene, aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard, and paperboard cartons. The company integrates recyclability into product development and supports increased use of recycled content, including recycled PET. Fuel, electricity, and natural gas are essential commodities due to their use in operations and transportation. Specialists secure supplies, and no significant continuous shortages have been experienced; many inputs are purchased in the open market, with prices subject to fluctuation managed through fixed-price contracts, purchase orders, pricing agreements, and derivative instruments like swaps and futures. Supply risks are mitigated by sourcing from multiple geographies and suppliers. Price increases may or may not be passed on to customers. Investments are made to improve the sustainability of agricultural supply chains, including expanding sustainable farming practices globally. In 2021, higher-than-anticipated input costs and limited shortages occurred due to global inflation, supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, increased demand, and pandemic-related regulatory and macroeconomic factors, continuing into fiscal 2022. The company maintains voluntary supply chain finance agreements with global financial institutions, allowing suppliers to sell their receivables to these institutions, which had no material impact on business or financial results. The company owns numerous trademarks essential to its global operations, including Agusha, Amp Energy, Aquafina, Arto Lifewtr, BaiCaoWei, Bare, Bokomo, Bolt24, bubly, Cap’n Crunch, Ceres, Cheetos, Chester’s, Chipita, Chipsy, Chokis, Chudo, Cracker Jack, Crunchy, Diet Mountain Dew, Diet Mug, Diet Pepsi, Diet 7UP (outside the U.S.), Domik v Derevne, Doritos, Driftwell, Duyvis, Elma Chips, Emperador, Evolve, Frito-Lay, Fritos, Fruktovy Sad, G2, Gamesa, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Gatorlyte, Grandma’s, H2oh!, Health Warrior, Imunele, J7, Kas, Kurkure, Lay’s, Life, Lifewtr, Liquifruit, Lubimy, Mabel, Manzanita Sol, Marias Gamesa, Matutano, Mirinda, Miss Vickie’s, Moirs, Mother’s, Mountain Dew, Mountain Dew Code Red, Mountain Dew Game Fuel, Mountain Dew Kickstart, Mountain Dew Zero Sugar, MTN Dew Energy, Mug, Munchies, Muscle Milk, Near East, Off the Eaten Path, Paso de los Toros, Pasta Roni, Pearl Milling Company, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, Pepsi Max, Pepsi Zero Sugar, PopCorners, Pronutro, Propel, Quaker, Quaker Chewy, Quaker Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni, Rockstar Energy, Rold Gold, Ruffles, Sabritas, Safari, Sakata, Saladitas, San Carlos, Sandora, Santitas, Sasko, 7UP (outside the U.S.), 7UP Free (outside the U.S.), Sierra Mist, Sierra Mist Zero Sugar, Simba, Smartfood, Smith’s, Snack a Jacks, SoBe, SodaStream, Sonric’s, Spekko, Stacy’s, Sting, Stubborn Soda, SunChips, Toddy, Toddynho, Tostitos, V Water, Vesely Molochnik, Walkers, Weetbix, White Star, Ya, and Yachak. The company holds long-term licenses to use certain trademarks in specific markets, including Ocean Spray. It distributes Bang Energy drinks and various Keurig Dr Pepper Inc. brands, including Dr Pepper, Crush, and Schweppes in certain markets. Joint ventures in which the company has an ownership interest own or have rights to use trademarks such as Lipton, Sabra, and Starbucks. In the first quarter of 2022, the company sold its Tropicana, Naked, and other select juice brands to PAI Partners while retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in a newly formed joint venture operating across North America and Europe. In the U.S., PepsiCo acts as the exclusive distributor for the joint venture’s portfolio for small-format and foodservice customers with chilled direct-store-delivery. In 2022, the company will begin distributing Hard MTN Dew, an alcoholic beverage manufactured and owned by the Boston Beer Company, and has licensed the Hard MTN Dew trademark to Boston Beer Company, which has appointed the company as its distributor. Trademarks remain valid as long as they are used properly for identification, and the company emphasizes correct use. The company authorizes the use of its trademarks in joint ventures, bottling appointments, and retail merchandise to enhance brand awareness. The company owns or has licenses to use patents related to products, packaging, production processes, and equipment design and operation, some of which are licensed to others. Sales are seasonally affected, with peak performance in the third quarter due to holiday patterns and lowest activity in the first quarter, though seasonality has not materially impacted consolidated financial results. Customers include wholesale and other distributors, foodservice providers, grocery stores, drug stores, convenience stores, discount/dollar stores, mass merchandisers, membership stores, hard discounters, e-commerce retailers, and authorized independent bottlers. Independent bottlers typically receive exclusive contracts to sell and manufacture certain beverage products in specific geographic areas, granting the company the right to charge royalties for concentrate, finished goods, and Aquafina, and specifying required manufacturing processes to ensure quality. Distribution rights are also granted to independent bottlers for certain beverage products in defined geographic areas. The company provides financial incentives to customers, including volume-based rebates, product placement fees, promotions, and displays for independent distributors and retailers. For independent bottlers, incentives—referred to as bottler funding—are negotiated annually and support consumer incentives, advertising, new product launches, and vending and cooler equipment placement. Consumer incentives include pricing discounts and promotions, advertising support includes media programs for bottler marketing, new product support includes targeted consumer and retailer incentives and point-of-purchase materials, and vending and cooler equipment programs support the acquisition and placement of vending machines. The nature and type of programs vary annually. Changes in the retail landscape, including retail consolidation, growth in e-commerce and subscription services, integration of physical and digital operations, international expansion of hard discounters, and the economic environment—including the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic—have increased the importance of major customers. In 2021, sales to Walmart Inc. (Walmart) and its affiliates, including Sam’s Club (Sam’s), represented approximately 13% of consolidated net revenue across all divisions, including concentrate sales to bottlers used in finished goods sold to Walmart. Losing this customer would have a material adverse effect on the FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA divisions. The company competes in highly competitive beverage and convenient food markets against international companies operating in multiple regions, regional and local manufacturers, private label brands, and smaller companies selling micro-brands directly via e-commerce or locally-focused retailers. In the United States, The Coca-Cola Company is the primary beverage competitor. Other competitors include Campbell Soup Company, Conagra Brands, Inc., Hormel Foods Corporation, Kellogg Company, Keurig Dr Pepper Inc., The Kraft Heinz Company, Link Snacks, Inc., Mondelēz International, Inc., Monster Beverage Corporation, Nestlé S.A., Red Bull GmbH, and Utz Brands, Inc. Many convenient food products hold significant market leadership in the U.S. and globally. In 2021, the company and The Coca-Cola Company represented approximately 22% and 19%, respectively, of the U.S. liquid refreshment beverage category by estimated retail sales in measured channels, according to Information Resources, Inc. However, The Coca-Cola Company has a significant carbonated soft drink share advantage in many markets outside the U.S. Competition is based on brand recognition, loyalty, taste, price, value, quality, product variety, innovation, distribution, advertising, marketing, packaging, convenience, service, and the ability to anticipate and respond to consumer preferences, including health and wellness and sustainability, as well as e-commerce trends. Success depends on effective promotion, new product development and reformulations, production efficiency, technology integration, advertising, marketing, packaging, pricing, vending equipment, and brand development. The company believes its brand strength, innovation, marketing, product quality, and flexible distribution network enable effective competition. The company conducts global research and development to meet customer and consumer needs and accelerate growth, focusing on creating preferred products through new technologies, ingredients, flavors, and substrates; improving manufacturing processes to reduce costs and environmental impact; reducing added sugars, sodium, or saturated fat; offering products with functional ingredients like whole grains, fruits, vegetables, dairy, protein, fiber, micronutrients, and hydration; developing sustainable packaging, including recyclable, compostable, biodegradable, or otherwise sustainable options and reducing plastic use; improving marketing, merchandising, and dispensing equipment; expanding beyond the bottle portfolio, including for SodaStream; investing in technology and digitalization such as artificial intelligence and data analytics for consumer insights; strengthening omnichannel capabilities, especially in e-commerce; and reducing environmental impact through reduced water use and climate impact across the value chain. Research centers are located globally in Brazil, China, India, Ireland, Mexico, Russia, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States, leveraging consumer insights, food science, and engineering to innovate the beverage and convenient food portfolio. The company’s operations are subject to various federal, state, and local laws in the U.S. and in over 200 other countries and territories, including the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, Food Safety Modernization Act, Occupational Safety and Health Act, environmental protection laws, Federal Motor Carrier Safety Act, Federal Trade Commission Act, Lanham Act, competition and trade practices laws, employment laws such as the Equal Employment Opportunity Act and Fair Labor Standards Act, alcohol sale and distribution laws, data privacy laws including the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 and California Privacy Rights Act, customs and foreign trade laws, school product regulations, supply chain laws such as the 2010 California Transparency in Supply Chains Act, tax laws, and the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act. The company also complies with state and local statutes, including Proposition 65 in California, which requires a warning on products containing substances known to cause cancer or birth defects unless below a safe harbor level.

PepsiCo is subject to a wide range of federal, state, and international laws and regulations that govern various aspects of its operations. These include the Equal Employment Opportunity Act, the National Labor Relations Act, and the Fair Labor Standards Act, which relate to employment and overtime compensation; laws concerning the sale and distribution of alcohol beverages; data privacy and personal data protection regulations, such as the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 and the California Privacy Rights Act; customs and foreign trade laws, including import/export regulations and tariffs; laws restricting the sale of certain products in schools; supply chain regulations, such as the 2010 California Transparency in Supply Chains Act; and laws related to tax payments. The company must also comply with the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and the Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act. Additionally, PepsiCo is subject to state and local statutes, including Proposition 65 in California, which requires warnings on products containing substances known to cause cancer or birth defects if above a safe harbor level. Outside the United States, the company faces numerous laws related to food safety, international trade, supply chain, occupational health and safety, competition, anti-corruption (including the U.K. Bribery Act), and data privacy (such as the European Union General Data Protection Regulation). Compliance with competition and anti-corruption laws is particularly important due to PepsiCo’s competitive position in many jurisdictions. The company relies on legal and operational compliance programs, in-house and external legal counsel, and other experts to ensure adherence to global laws. Certain jurisdictions have imposed or are considering imposing new or increased taxes on the manufacture, distribution, or sale of PepsiCo’s products, ingredients, or substances, with tax structures varying—some applying to all beverages, including non-caloric ones, while others target beverages with caloric sweeteners, using single, graduated, or flat tax rates based on sugar content. Some jurisdictions have also introduced or are considering product labeling, warning, or marketing restrictions, such as highlighting health concerns, warning against certain ingredients, restricting sales to specific age groups, or limiting product availability. Similar or more restrictive measures may be proposed in the future. PepsiCo is also subject to environmental laws in the U.S. and abroad, including the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act, and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, as well as similar regulations outside the U.S. Concerns over environmental, social, and governance issues, including climate change, are leading to new or stricter requirements to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, limit commercial water use, and mandate reporting of environmental metrics. PepsiCo adheres to all applicable environmental laws, maintains global environmental compliance programs, and makes necessary expenditures for compliance and sustainability goals. While these costs have not materially impacted its business, financial condition, or operations, future changes in environmental regulations or compliance costs could adversely affect financial performance. The company also faces environmental remediation and indemnification obligations from historical activities or acquired businesses, which, though not currently material, cannot be predicted with certainty. PepsiCo employs approximately 309,000 people worldwide as of December 25, 2021, including about 129,000 in the United States, and is party to numerous collective bargaining agreements, with generally good employee relations. Protecting employee safety, health, and well-being is a top priority, with investments in technologies like fleet telematics, distracted driving prevention, and wearable ergonomic devices to reduce workplace injuries. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the company maintained health and safety protocols, provided personal protective equipment, and enabled testing, especially for frontline workers. PepsiCo believes its culture of diversity, equity, and inclusion is a competitive advantage, enhancing innovation, talent attraction, and reputation. As of December 25, 2021, 27% of the global workforce was female, with 43% of management roles held by women; 45% of the U.S. workforce was racially/ethnically diverse, and 31% of U.S. managerial roles were held by racially/ethnically diverse individuals. Seven of the CEO’s direct reports are racially/ethnically diverse or female. The company supports associate development through global training and development programs, including career plans, mentoring, and in-house learning such as PEP U Degreed, with over 1,000,000 training hours completed in 2021. PepsiCo files annual, quarterly, and current reports, proxy statements, and other disclosures with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and these filings are available on the SEC’s website at http://www.sec.gov. The company also makes its reports available free of charge on its corporate website at http://www.pepsico.com as soon as reasonably practicable after filing. Investors are encouraged to review information posted on these platforms, which may be deemed material, and the company may update its communication channels, with such changes posted on its website. Information on the website is not incorporated into or part of any SEC filing. The document also includes a section on risk factors, noting that ongoing uncertainty from the COVID-19 pandemic continues to affect business operations, including changes in consumer demand, shifts in channel preferences (such as increased e-commerce), supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, and rising operational costs due to remote work, PPE, sanitation, and inflation. The pandemic has also increased vulnerability to cyberattacks and disrupted information technology infrastructure. Economic uncertainty has affected access to capital and credit markets. Reduced demand for products due to shifts in consumer preferences—such as changes in demographics, pricing, product quality, packaging concerns, or nutrition-related perceptions—can lead to reduced sales, inventory write-offs, or eroded competitiveness. Damage to the company’s reputation, due to ethical, environmental, social, or governance failures, product safety issues, advertising controversies, or social media responses, can decrease demand and harm business performance. Product recalls, due to mislabeling, spoilage, allergens, adulteration, or contamination, can result in financial losses, inventory destruction, lost sales, and reduced consumer confidence, while failures in quality oversight may lead to litigation, investigations, fines, or criminal liability. Consumer loss of confidence in product quality or safety can also negatively impact the business.

Product recalls due to quality or safety issues—such as mislabeling, misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration, or contamination—can negatively impact the business by causing financial losses, destroying inventory, and leading to lost sales during periods of product unavailability. Such issues, whether stemming from non-compliance with food safety laws or other causes, may also erode consumer confidence, reduce demand, disrupt production and delivery, increase costs including fines or judgments, and harm the company’s reputation, especially as it expands into new categories like nuts and meat convenient foods globally and the distribution of alcoholic beverages in the United States. Failure to maintain proper oversight of product quality or safety can lead to recalls, litigation, government investigations, or civil or criminal proceedings, resulting in fines, penalties, damages, or liability. Even if unrelated to specific products, a general loss of consumer confidence in product quality, safety, or integrity can adversely affect the business. The company competes with international beverage and convenient food firms, regional and local manufacturers, private label brands, and small businesses selling micro brands via e-commerce or local retailers. In many markets, including the United States, The Coca-Cola Company is the primary beverage competitor. Competition is based on brand recognition, loyalty, taste, price, value, quality, product variety, innovation, distribution, advertising, marketing, packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to consumer trends. Business performance can be harmed if the company fails to promote or develop existing products, introduce and market new ones effectively, adopt new technologies like artificial intelligence and data analytics, strengthen digital marketing capabilities, or respond to supply disruptions, pricing pressure, or competitive actions. Failure to attract, develop, and retain a highly skilled and diverse workforce—particularly in areas like e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics—can deplete institutional knowledge, erode competitive advantages, increase employee costs, and damage reputation, especially if underrepresented communities are not adequately supported. Water scarcity, due to limited availability, climate change, or increasing regulatory and consumer pressure, can disrupt supply chains, affect operations, raise compliance and production costs, lead to facility interruptions or relocations, hinder water use goals, damage the company’s environmental image, or harm its reputation. Changes in the retail landscape—such as growth in e-commerce and hard discounters—can negatively affect the business if the company fails to maintain strong relationships with these channels or traditional retailers, especially as key customers increase their e-commerce sales. Expanding direct-to-consumer e-commerce capabilities profitably is also a challenge. Retail consolidation in North America, Europe, and Latin America, where large buyers have increased purchasing power, can reduce the company’s competitiveness and weaken smaller customers’ ability to purchase products, leading to lost orders or reduced payments. Maintaining strong relationships with key customers, such as Walmart, is essential; disputes, changes in their financial condition, significant sales declines, or customer loss can harm the business. Disruptions in manufacturing or supply chains—due to civil unrest, political instability, limited supplier availability, or seasonal shortages—can increase costs and interrupt product supply. Raw materials, including agricultural commodities, fuel, packaging (like recycled PET), transportation, labor, and other inputs are subject to price volatility and supply fluctuations from factors such as demand changes, inflation, weather, disease (e.g., greening disease in citrus), labor shortages (e.g., truck drivers), strikes, tariffs, trade barriers, port congestion, cybersecurity incidents, political uncertainty, terrorism, or currency fluctuations. Many raw materials are purchased in the open market, and unexpected or significant price increases may prevent the company from raising product prices or hedging effectively, leading to reduced revenue, margins, and operating results. Political and social conditions—such as election outcomes, government shutdowns, hostilities, or protests—can create uncertainty in regulations, tariffs, environmental policies, tax laws, and currency exchange rates, affecting demand and operations. In certain U.S. and global cities, prolonged protests or demonstrations, especially related to elections or civil rights, may disrupt operations, including distribution and raw material supply, due to government actions. Growth in developing and emerging markets—such as Mexico, Russia, the Middle East, China, South Africa, Brazil, and India—depends on product acceptance, cultural fit, distribution methods, and market conditions, but these markets face risks including economic instability, political unrest, war, terrorism, sanctions, foreign ownership restrictions, nationalization, government-mandated closures, import/export restrictions, currency devaluation or demonetization, complex compliance with laws like the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act or the U.K. Bribery Act, and weak legal systems. Failure to expand successfully or manage these risks can reduce returns on capital. Unfavorable economic conditions—such as recessions, inflation, volatile commodity markets, labor shortages, credit contraction, or currency fluctuations—can impact interest rates, taxes, pension costs, and overall financial stability, affecting both the company and its business partners. Future cyber incidents—such as cyberattacks, ransomware, denial-of-service attacks, social engineering, or supply chain compromises through software updates or compromised supplier accounts—can disrupt operations, compromise data, lead to financial losses, litigation, regulatory investigations, fines, reputational damage, or employee morale issues. These risks extend to third-party providers, including suppliers and cloud service providers, whose systems or failures can indirectly impact the company. Although past incidents have not materially affected operations, future events could have significant consequences. Despite investments in network security, disaster recovery, and employee training, there is no guarantee that systems will be fully protected. Insurance may cover some costs but may not cover all losses or reputational damage. Strategic transactions—such as acquisitions, joint ventures, divestitures, or distribution agreements—carry risks including failure to achieve expected synergies, delays in approvals, difficulties in integrating operations or IT systems, challenges in retaining key personnel, maintaining compliance with internal controls and anti-bribery laws, managing tax costs, preserving customer relationships, or handling differing interests among joint venture partners.

The success of strategic transactions, including the recent completion of the Juice Transaction, depends on our ability to realize expected returns, benefits, cost savings, or synergies within the anticipated time frame or at all, as well as receiving necessary consents, clearances, and approvals. Risks associated with such transactions include difficulties in integrating manufacturing, distribution, sales, accounting, financial reporting, and administrative support activities and information technology systems with our company, or in separating such personnel, activities, and systems during divestitures; operating under new business models or in new categories or territories; motivating, recruiting, and retaining executives and key employees; conforming controls (including internal control over financial reporting and disclosure controls and procedures) and policies (including environmental, health and safety, and anti-bribery compliance); retaining existing customers and attracting new ones; managing tax costs or inefficiencies; maintaining good relations with divested or refranchised businesses in our supply or sales chain; offsetting revenue losses from divested brands or businesses; managing the impact of decisions or actions by joint venture partners with differing interests; and other unanticipated problems or liabilities, such as contingent liabilities and litigation. Failure to successfully complete or manage these transactions or to effectively manage associated risks can have adverse effects on our business. Our reliance on third-party service providers—such as cloud data providers for payroll processing, health and benefit administration, and finance and accounting functions—can negatively impact our business. If these providers fail to meet their contractual, regulatory, or other obligations or if we inadequately monitor their performance, we may fail to achieve expected cost savings or efficiencies, incur additional costs to correct errors, experience business disruption, systems performance degradation, processing inefficiencies, security breaches leading to loss or damage of intellectual property or sensitive data, incorrect or adverse financial reporting, litigation, claims, regulatory proceedings, fines, penalties, remediation costs, reputational damage, or negative employee morale—all of which can harm our business. We are also advancing a multi-year phased business transformation to migrate financial processing systems to enterprise-wide solutions, which has led to and could continue to result in systems outages and operating inefficiencies. If we fail to allocate and manage sufficient resources to build and sustain the necessary information technology infrastructure or fail to achieve expected benefits from this initiative, our business could be adversely affected. Climate change poses risks to our business and reputation, as it may reduce agricultural productivity and availability or increase pricing for key commodities like potatoes, sugar cane, corn, wheat, rice, oats, oranges, and fruit-derived oils; it may also increase the frequency or severity of natural disasters and extreme weather, impairing production, disrupting supply chains, or affecting product demand. Additionally, many jurisdictions are implementing environmental policies related to climate change, greenhouse gas emissions, energy use, and sustainability—including single-use plastics—leading to new or increased legal and regulatory requirements, such as carbon pricing, which could significantly raise costs and require additional investments in facilities and equipment. Failure to meet environmental goals or perceived inaction on climate change can lead to adverse publicity, reducing product demand and damaging our reputation. Strikes or work stoppages, due to collective bargaining agreements, can impair manufacturing and distribution, lead to lost sales, increased costs, and hinder operational changes or strategic adaptation, all of which can negatively affect our business. Financial risks include failure to realize benefits from productivity initiatives, such as shared service models, which may result in business disruptions, employee distraction, reduced morale, unexpected attrition, difficulty attracting or retaining key personnel, and negative publicity—leading to adverse financial performance if expected savings are not achieved. A deterioration in assumptions about future business performance, such as competitive or macroeconomic conditions or changes in the weighted-average cost of capital, can trigger impairment charges that harm results of operations. Exchange rate fluctuations, due to inflation, monetary policies, currency controls, or restrictions, impact financial performance because our consolidated financial statements are in U.S. dollars, and we pay for raw materials and ingredients in multiple currencies. A downgrade or potential downgrade of our credit ratings—based on factors like cash generation, indebtedness, shareholder distributions, and broader economic or industry conditions—can increase borrowing costs, impair access to capital and credit markets, reduce liquidity, and limit access to commercial paper, forcing reliance on more expensive debt financing, all of which can harm financial performance. Legal, tax, and regulatory risks include taxes on products, particularly beverages, imposed or considered in jurisdictions like Canada, where a flat tax of 0.20 Canadian dollars (0.16 U.S. dollars) per liter on sugar-sweetened beverages was enacted on September 1, 2022, which can increase product costs, reduce consumption, and lead to negative publicity. Limitations on marketing or sale, such as warning labels in Argentina and Colombia requiring disclosure of high sugar, sodium, or saturated fat content, or color-coded labeling, can reduce consumption, cause negative publicity, or lead consumers to believe our products do not meet health needs. Laws and regulations on plastics or packaging, including extended producer responsibility, plastic taxes, bans on single-use plastics, bottle cap tethering, and minimum recycled content requirements (e.g., in the European Union, Peru, and U.S. states), can increase product costs, affect demand, result in negative publicity, and require investments in alternative or less plastic packaging. Failure to comply with personal data protection laws—such as the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation and California’s California Consumer Privacy Act—can lead to litigation, fines, penalties, and reputational damage due to inconsistent or evolving regulations. Increases in income tax rates, changes in tax laws, or disagreements with tax authorities—especially amid global proposals for a 15% minimum tax rate and profit reallocation—can increase tax uncertainty, compliance costs, and adverse financial impacts, particularly as tax audits and disputes may result in outcomes different from historical provisions. If we fail to protect our intellectual property—such as ingredient formulas, trademarks, patents, or trade secrets—our competitive position and product value could be reduced, and we may face litigation, damages, injunctions, inventory write-offs, or restrictions on product development or sales due to past or future infringement claims. Our business is subject to numerous laws and regulations covering production, storage, distribution, labeling, advertising, quality, safety, packaging, environmental, social, and governance matters, including climate change, and compliance with competition and anti-corruption laws. New laws, regulatory changes, or differing standards across markets can increase compliance and production costs. For example, growing societal attention to environmental, social, and governance issues has led to new regulations, and entering new markets—such as the U.S. alcoholic beverage distribution or global nuts and meat convenient foods—exposes us to additional regulatory burdens. If one jurisdiction imposes new regulations affecting our products, others may follow. Non-compliance can result in criminal or civil actions, including fines, injunctions, product recalls, penalties, disgorgement, or activity restrictions. Additionally, third-party studies—regardless of scientific validity—on the health effects of ingredients or packaging have led to or could lead to new taxes, regulations, or lawsuits that adversely affect our business. Potential liabilities and costs from litigation remain a significant risk.

Increasing governmental and societal attention to environmental, social, and governance issues has led to and may continue to lead to new laws or regulatory requirements. The entry into new markets or product categories, such as the planned entry into the alcoholic beverage industry as a distributor in the United States and expansion into the nuts and meat convenient foods categories globally, has resulted in and could continue to result in additional regulations, increasing compliance costs. If one jurisdiction introduces or proposes new laws or regulations affecting the manufacture, distribution, or sale of the company’s products, other jurisdictions may follow. Failure to comply with such laws or regulations can result in criminal or civil enforcement actions, including fines, injunctions, product recalls, penalties, disgorgement of profits, or activity restrictions, all of which could negatively impact the business. Responding to these matters—even if ultimately non-meritorious—requires significant expense and resource allocation and may lead to adverse publicity that harms the company’s reputation or brand image. As of February 3, 2022, there were approximately 101,778 shareholders of record. PepsiCo has paid consecutive quarterly cash dividends since 1965, with dividends typically declared in February, May, July, and November and paid at the end of March, June, September, and the beginning of January. On February 2, 2022, the Board declared a quarterly dividend of $1.075 per share payable March 31, 2022, to shareholders of record on March 4, 2022. For the remainder of 2022, record dates were expected to be June 3, September 2, and December 2, 2022, subject to Board approval. On February 10, 2022, PepsiCo announced a 7% increase in its annualized dividend to $4.60 per share from $4.30 per share, effective with the dividend to be paid in June 2022. Additionally, on February 10, 2022, the company announced a share repurchase program authorizing the repurchase of up to $10.0 billion of PepsiCo common stock, commencing on February 11, 2022, and expiring on February 28, 2026. Shares may be repurchased in open market transactions, privately negotiated transactions, accelerated stock repurchases, or otherwise. PepsiCo expects to return approximately $7.7 billion to shareholders in 2022, consisting of dividends of approximately $6.2 billion and share repurchases of approximately $1.5 billion.
